question.text: Consider the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix},\mathbf{a}_2=\begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix},$ and $\mathbf{a}_3=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}.$ Find a basis of $S=\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}$ by inspection.
question.explanation:
Remember that a basis of $S$ is a set of linearly independent vectors that spans $S.$

From the given vectors, we can see that $\mathbf{a}_2$ is a linear combination of vectors $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_3\mathbin{:}$

\[ \mathbf{a}_2=1\cdot \mathbf{a}_1+1 \cdot \mathbf{a}_3 \]

Consequently, the vector $\mathbf{a}_2$ can be removed from $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}$ without changing the span. So $S = \textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}$ is spanned by just $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_3\}.$

Lastly, note that $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_3$ are linearly independent since they are not parallel. So the set $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_3\}$ is a linearly independent set that spans $S.$

Therefore, a basis of $S$ is $\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_3\},$ that is to say,

\[ \mathcal{B} = \Bigg\{ \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_1}, \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}}_{\color{black}\mathbf{a}_3} \Bigg\}. \]

question.text: Consider the vectors $\mathbf{a}_1=\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix},$ $\mathbf{a}_2=\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 7 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix},$ and $\mathbf{a}_3=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -14 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}.$ Find a basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}.$
question.explanation:
We need to find a subset of linearly independent vectors. So, we start by creating a matrix whose columns are made up of our vectors, and then we reduce the matrix to row echelon form:

\begin{align*} \phantom{M} &\phantom{=\:\,} \begin{bmatrix} 5 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 7 & -14 \\ 0 & 0 & 0 \\ \end{bmatrix} \end{align*}

In this case, our matrix is already in a row echelon form.

The pivot columns correspond to linearly independent vectors, while the non-pivot columns correspond to linearly dependent vectors that can be removed. Here, the $1$st and $2$nd columns are pivot columns, while the $3$rd column is a non-pivot column.

The $1$st and $2$nd columns from the original matrix are $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_2.$ So, a basis of $S$ is $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \},$ that is to say,

\[ \mathcal{B}=\left\{ \begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 0 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 7 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\right\}. \]

The $1$st and $3$rd columns from the original matrix are $\mathbf{a}_1$ and $\mathbf{a}_3.$ So, a basis of $S$ is $\{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_3 \},$ that is to say,

question.text: The vectors $\mathbf{a}_1,$ $\mathbf{a}_2,$ and $\mathbf{a}_3$ are given below. Determine whether $\mathcal{B} = \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ is a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}.$ If that is the case, find $x_1 \cdot x_2,$ where $\mathbf{a}_3=x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2.$ \[ \mathbf{a}_1=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{a}_2=\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{a}_3=\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
We want to determine if $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}.$ So, we want to find $x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that \[ {\color{black}x_1} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_1} + {\color{rblack}x_2} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_2} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_3}. \]

This equation is equivalent to the system \[ \begin{cases} x_1-x_2 = 2 \\ -2x_1+4x_2 = -2 \end{cases} \]

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

\begin{align*} \phantom{A} &\phantom{=}\:\, \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ -2 & 4 & -2 \end{array}\right] & R_2 &:= R_2+2R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 2 & 2 \end{array}\right] & R_2&:=\dfrac{1}{2} R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & -1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{array}\right] & R_1&:=R_1+R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 0 & 3 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{array}\right] \end{align*}

From the RREF matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}.$ Also, the matrix tells us that $x_1=3$ and $x_2=1,$ meaning that \[ 3 \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_1} + 1 \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -1 \\ 4 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_2} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ -2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_3}. \]

Therefore, $x_1 \cdot x_2 = 3 \cdot 1 = 3.$

question.text: The vectors $\mathbf{a}_1,$ $\mathbf{a}_2,$ and $\mathbf{a}_3$ are given below. question.explanation:
We want to determine if $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}.$ So, we want to find $x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that \[ {\color{black}x_1} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_1} + {\color{rblack}x_2} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_2} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 14 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_3}. \]

This equation is equivalent to the system \[ \begin{cases} 2x_1-2x_2 = 14 \\ 2x_1-x_2 = 9 \end{cases} \]

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

\begin{align*} \phantom{A} &\phantom{=}\:\, \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 2 & -2 & 14 \\ 2 & -1 & 9 \end{array}\right] & R_1 &:= \dfrac{1}{2}R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & -1 & 7 \\ 2 & -1 & 9 \end{array}\right] & R_2&:= R_2 + (-2)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & -1 & 7 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 \end{array}\right] & R_1&:=R_1+R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & -5 \end{array}\right] \end{align*}

From the RREF matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}.$ Also, the matrix tells us that $x_1=2$ and $x_2=-5,$ meaning that \[ 2 \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 2 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_1} + (-5) \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -2 \\ -1 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_2} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 14 \\ 9 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_3}. \]

Therefore, $x_1 \cdot x_2 = 2 \cdot (-5) = -10.$

question.text: The vectors $\mathbf{a}_1,$ $\mathbf{a}_2,$ $\mathbf{a}_3,$ and $\mathbf{a}_4$ are given below. Determine whether $\mathcal{B} = \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2, \mathbf{a}_3 \}$ is a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3, \mathbf{a}_4 \}.$ If that is the case, find $x_1 + x_2 + x_3,$ where $\mathbf{a}_4=x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2+x_3\mathbf{a}_3.$ \[ \mathbf{a}_1=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{a}_2=\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{a}_3=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{a}_4=\begin{bmatrix} -7 \\ -21 \\ -52 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
We want to determine if $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3,\mathbf{a}_4 \}.$ So, we want to find $x_1, x_2, x_3 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that \[ {\color{black}x_1} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_1} + {\color{rblack}x_2} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_2} + {\color{rblack}x_3} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_3} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -7 \\ -21 \\ -52 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_4}. \]

This equation is equivalent to the system \[ \begin{cases} x_1+x_3 = -7 \\ 3x_1+x_2+3x_3 = -21 \\ 7x_1+8x_3 = -52 \end{cases} \]

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

\begin{align*} \phantom{A} &\phantom{=}\:\, \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 0 & 1 & -7 \\ 3 & 1 & 3 & -21 \\ 7 & 0 & 8 & -52 \end{array}\right] & R_2&:= R_2 + (-3)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 0 & 1 & -7 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 7 & 0 & 8 & -52 \end{array}\right] & R_3&:=R_3+(-7)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 0 & 1 & -7 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3 \end{array}\right] & R_1&:=R_1+(-1)R_3 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{ccc|c} 1 & 0 & 0 & -4 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & 0 & 1 & -3 \end{array}\right] \end{align*}

From the reduced matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st, $2$nd, and $3$rd columns. So, $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3,\mathbf{a}_4 \}.$ Also, the matrix tells us that $x_1=-4,$ $x_2=0,$ and $x_3=-3,$ meaning that \[ (-4) \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_1} + 0 \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 0 \\ 1 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_2} + (-3) \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \\ 8 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_3} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} -7 \\ -21 \\ -52 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_4}. \]

Therefore, $x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = (-4) + 0 + (-3) = -7.$

example.title: Determining Whether a Given Set Is a Basis of a Span

question.text: The vectors $\mathbf{a}_1,$ $\mathbf{a}_2,$ and $\mathbf{a}_3$ are given below. Determine whether $\mathcal{B} = \{ \mathbf{a}_1, \mathbf{a}_2 \}$ is a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}.$ If that is the case, find $x_1 \cdot x_2,$ where $\mathbf{a}_3=x_1\mathbf{a}_1+x_2\mathbf{a}_2.$ \[ \mathbf{a}_1=\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{a}_2=\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}, \qquad \mathbf{a}_3=\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 17 \end{bmatrix} \]
question.explanation:
We want to determine if $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}.$ So, we want to find $x_1, x_2 \in \mathbb{R}$ such that \[ {\color{black}x_1} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_1} + {\color{rblack}x_2} \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_2} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 17 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_3}. \]

This equation is equivalent to the system \[ \begin{cases} x_1+3x_2 = 5 \\ 5x_1+5x_2 = 17 \end{cases} \]

Now, we reduce the augmented matrix of the system to reduced row echelon form (RREF):

\begin{align*} \phantom{A} &\phantom{=}\:\, \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 5 & 7 & 17 \end{array}\right] & R_2 &:= R_2+(-5)R_1 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & -8 & -8 \end{array}\right] & R_2&:=-\dfrac{1}{8} R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 3 & 5 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{array}\right] & R_1&:=R_1+(-3)R_2 \\[5pt] &\sim \left[\begin{array}{cc|c} 1 & 0 & 2 \\ 0 & 1 & 1 \end{array}\right] \end{align*}

From the RREF matrix above, we see that the pivot columns are the $1$st and $2$nd columns. So, $\mathcal{B}$ is indeed a basis of $\textrm{Span}\{\mathbf{a}_1,\mathbf{a}_2,\mathbf{a}_3 \}.$ Also, the matrix tells us that $x_1=2$ and $x_2=1,$ meaning that \[ 2 \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 1 \\ 5 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_1} + 1 \cdot \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ 7 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_2} = \underbrace{\begin{bmatrix} 5 \\ 17 \end{bmatrix}}_{\mathbf{a}_3}. \]

Therefore, $x_1 \cdot x_2 = 2 \cdot 1 = 2.$
